📊 📉 Europe's rearmament plans face energy price surge, cold winter and Norwegian supply disruptions European gas prices jumped as much as 8.6% on Monday, with Dutch TTF futures hitting €96.07 ($105.34) per megawatt-hour in their biggest intraday surge in over a week as winter demand peaks. As of November 24, the benchmark was trading above €90 per MWh, more than three times its level of around €29-30 a year earlier . European gas storage levels remain well below seasonal averages, Bloomberg warns, adding to upward price pressures as a cold snap across northwestern Europe is expected to persist into early December. To add insult to injury, three major Equinor-operated Norwegian fields — Troll, Visund and Asgard — have all faced production constraints at the same time, further tightening Europe's gas supply and pushing prices higher. Troll is described as the backbone of Norwegian production with roughly 40% of continental-shelf gas reserves and technical capacity 124-131 million cubic meters (mcm) per day. It suffered outages earlier this month that helped drive a 7% TTF spike. Even brief disruptions at Troll affect the market: Norway is currently Europe’s largest pipeline gas supplier. Visund remains fully shut until at least January 1, 2027, after a November 4 electrical-switchgear fire. The platform’s 13.2 mcm/day capacity is offline as extensive repairs continue. Asgard is still running around 5.7 mcm/day below capacity which is still an improvement from the 8.9 mcm/day shortfall reported late last week. Separately, Equinor disclosed a cyberattack on some IT systems, detected 17 November and largely contained by November 20. Against this backdrop, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte's reassurances at the 72nd Annual Session of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin — that even if war breaks out, Europe's lights will stay on, homes will remain warm and communications will keep working – don't sound entirely convincing to some European observers. Higher energy costs are also set to put additional pressure on Europe's industrial base just as Brussels is shifting it onto a war footing under the ReArm Europe 2030 plan . 👍 Substack | Chat | @geopolitics_prime

🇩🇪 🇺🇦 Ukrainian refugees in Germany lose benefits after income checks using the Diia app In the Greiz district of Thuringia, German authorities identified 54 Ukrainian refugees who had failed to declare income and assets held in Ukraine, Focus reports. As a result, 16 people had their social benefits withdrawn entirely, while payments to a further 38 recipients were reduced. According to the report, German authorities used Ukrainian documents obtained through the Diia digital government platform to cross-check information about pensions, rental income, bank accounts and other assets. Diia provided access to official records; it was not necessarily an automated data-sharing or surveillance system. What Kiev promoted as a flagship digital-government achievement has, in this case, reportedly helped German authorities verify financial disclosures and identify undeclared assets among benefit recipients. 🔴 @DDGeopolitics

Open Source Intel MORE INFO: Israel has shared intelligence with the US indicating that Iran is developing chemical weapons for potential use against Israel and other countries in the region, Defense Minister Israel Katz told reporters. He also confirmed that the IDF and U.S. Central Command have prepared plans for a joint strike on Iran. Chemical weapons. Katz said Iran sees chemical weapons as a potential “game-changer.” Israel has had the intelligence for some time, and its assessment is that Iran would use the weapons if it acquired them. Katz said Israel is determined to prevent that and must verify whether Iran has begun production. How urgent is the threat? “If we thought this was already an imminent event, we would have acted,” Katz said. The nuclear program. Katz said Iran is working to revive its nuclear program. In Israel’s assessment, a chemical arsenal could deter Israel and other countries from intervening, giving Tehran more room to advance its nuclear work. Joint strike plans. Katz said plans for a joint operation are ready and the decision rests with President Trump. Israel prefers to coordinate with Washington but can strike independently if necessary. Katz said he, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the IDF chief of staff agree on that position. Trump considered a strike before Israel’s elections. According to Katz, Netanyahu told Trump that Israel wanted to avoid a strike before the vote. Trump later called it off. Katz said Trump also weighs the views of regional partners, energy interests and the prospects for an agreement with Iran. Iran could strike first. Katz acknowledged the risk of a preemptive Iranian attack and said Israel must be prepared to strike even under those circumstances. Threats on U.S. soil. Katz accused Iran of actively working to assassinate Trump and harm other senior U.S. officials inside the United States. Iran’s missile launchers. Katz linked the timing of any Israeli action to the difficulty of defending against Iranian fire. “The sooner we act to eliminate Iran’s missile-launch capabilities, the easier our defensive mission will be.” tweet
